The evidence located uses different definitions, tests, ages and thresholds. The editorial decision is not to turn that variation into a single worldwide percentage until a recent international synthesis with comparable methodology is available.

The important point on this page is methodological: no sufficiently comparable single global figure has been selected. Dyscalculia and dysgraphia are studied using different ages, tests, definitions and cut-off points; publishing a single percentage without explaining those differences would imply a precision that the selected evidence does not allow.
The publishable conclusion is precisely that no single global figure is selected. Do not fill this block with ranges from general-information pages that lack comparable methodology.
The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

The underlying research did not select a single source with robustness comparable to those used for ADHD, dyslexia or developmental coordination disorder. Before adding a figure, a recent international review must be found with explicit definition, population, method and cut-off criterion.

Anxiety disorders are the most common mental disorders worldwide. WHO estimates that in 2021 they affected 359 million people, including 72 million minors, and that around 27.6% of those who need treatment receive it.

WHO combines a global estimate of people with anxiety disorders in 2021 with an indicator of the treatment gap. The page distinguishes how many people are estimated to be affected from how many receive care among those who need it.
Cite 359 million and 4.4% as WHO estimates for 2021. If the 27.6% figure is used, clarify that it refers to the proportion of people who need treatment who receive some form of treatment.
Anxiety is not a synonym for neurodivergence. It is included because it often appears as a coexisting condition and because it is part of the Iris Green knowledge base.

There is no single global prevalence figure for OCD independent of diagnostic criteria. An international study published in 2026 estimated lifetime prevalence between 2.28% and 3.21%, depending on the diagnostic system used.
A systematic review and modelling study published online on 8 July 2026 brought together 112 studies representative of national or subnational populations.

The review estimates lifetime prevalence and shows that the result depends on the diagnostic system applied. The four figures do not compete with one another: each one corresponds to different criteria.
It shows that even the same condition can produce different figures depending on the criterion used. The statistical definition matters.
State that lifetime prevalence changes according to diagnostic criteria. The range 2.28–3.21% is not a confidence interval for a single figure.
The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.
